verses.verse:
ततोऽधिके च न्यूने च बंश खंडे प्रकल्पिते।
स्वासमानानुरोधेन मन्द्रतार व्यतिक्रमः।।१५।।
verses.text: If the piece of bamboo is made longer or shorter than that, then, in proportion to the breath, the lower and upper registers fall out of order.

commentary.text: For a bānsurī it is necessary that a note one saptaka (octave) higher than the note that sounds when the phūṅk (breath) is kept weak will sound when the breath is made strong. And for this one-octave difference to come out exactly on all seven notes, it is possible only if the length of the pipe or bamboo follows the rule given above, not otherwise. To test this I have blown and tried pieces of pipe from the smallest, whose length equalled the antaḥparidhimāna (measure of the inner circumference), up to the largest, which were 16 times that measure. The corrected measure that came out of this was then fixed. In any case, these days it is a problem for most bānsurī players where to buy a tuneful bānsurī. If someone has somehow trained his breath on an out-of-tune bānsurī, then even another, tuneful bānsurī will be out of tune for him.

Now it must be made clear here how the proper length stated for the bānsurī is valid. If you measure the antaḥparidhi (inner circumference), that is the inner girth, of a pipe and cut the pipe to just that length, then the length and width of the air inside it, which has to be set in motion by the breath, will become equal, and it cannot be set in motion by the breath; so only a bare sound (nāda) will arise in it. If its length is made four times, two sounds can be produced by the breath, about an octave apart. Now if a hole is made in the pipe at 5 times the length, two sounds exactly an octave apart can be produced. So it must be accepted that if we need two forms of each of the seven notes, one octave apart from each other by just lessening or increasing the breath, then for this a pipe of eight times will be right. For if one makes a mukharandhra (mouth-hole) in a pipe of eight times and blows, then as the vega (force) of the breath is raised step by step, 4 sounds of this kind are seen to arise: Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa. With skilful blowing one more sound will come, which we can call the G̈a of the ati-tāra saptaka (very high octave). This is the meaning of the following śloka.
